column1: # title: ENG-205 Middle Ages Intro — 1 Definitions

column2: The word medieval comes from the Latin medium, meaning middle, and aevum, meaning age. It names the 'middle age' between the fall of Rome and the Renaissance.
Old English, also called Anglo-Saxon, is the earliest form of the English language. It is a Germanic language that was heavily inflected, meaning its words changed their endings to show grammar.
Anglo-Norman is the form of Old French that was used in medieval England.
Middle English is the form of English that came after Old English. It had simpler grammar than Old English, thousands of words borrowed from French, and no single standard form.
Early Modern English is the form of English that came after Middle English and led directly to the English spoken today. Its spelling was largely fixed, and its long vowels sounded much like ours.
An inflected language is one in which words change their endings to show their function, such as person, number, tense, case and mood.
Alliteration is the repetition of the same starting sound at the beginning of several nearby words.
A kenning is a two-word compound noun used in place of a plain noun. For example, 'life-house' means the body and 'whale-road' means the sea.
Elegiac describes a mournful tone that laments loss and the passing of time.

In the heroic code, kinship rather than geography makes a nation, and the lord must be generous, giving his men gifts and treasure. In return his men owe him loyalty to the death and revenge after he dies, and scholars call this bond the comitatus.

Synecdoche and metonymy are figures of speech. In synecdoche a part stands for the whole, as when 'keel' means a ship, and in metonymy something closely associated with a thing stands in for it, as when 'crown' means the king.
Wergild was money paid to a victim's family by the person who caused a death, as compensation in place of blood revenge.
The Witan was the Anglo-Saxon council of nobles who advised the king.
The fyrd was the Anglo-Saxon national militia, an army of ordinary men called up to defend the kingdom.
A shire-reeve was the official who ran a shire, or county, for the king.
The Danelaw was the area of eastern Britain settled by the Vikings, or Danes, where Danish law rather than Anglo-Saxon law applied.
The Domesday Survey, or Domesday Book, was a census of all the land, people and property in England, right down to the livestock, made so the king could tax them.
Hagiography is writing about the lives of saints.
A Breton lay is a short Celtic tale of love and adventure that was sung by storytellers.
A chivalric romance is a story of knightly adventure, courtly love and courtesy toward ladies, and martial prowess against powerful foes.
The Alliterative Revival was a return to Old English-style alliterative verse in Middle English poetry.
A mystery play is a medieval play that dramatizes a Bible story as part of a cycle of plays. A morality play is an allegorical play in which personified virtues and vices fight for a person's soul.
The Black Death was a deadly epidemic of bubonic plague.
The Great Vowel Shift was a major change in how English long vowels were pronounced.
The Exeter Book is a large manuscript collection of Old English poetry, including many riddles.
Beowulf is an Old English heroic epic, a long narrative poem celebrating the deeds of the warrior hero Beowulf.
